newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria to complete dinar convertibility in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Algeria to complete dinar convertibility in 1998.

text.p: Algeria's Central Bank governor Abdelwahab Keramane said financial and monetary moves to turn the dinar into a fully convertible currency will be completed in 1998 when Algeria will join the World Trade Organisation.

"The dinar convertibility for current operations and Algeria's membership of the World Trade Organisation would be perfected in 1998," he was quoted saying in reports published Monday by official media and newspapers.
The Algerian dinar is partially convertible, mostly for import and export trade operations.

Keramane, who made his remarks to a closed-door meeting of the government-appointed Transitional National Council (CNT) on Sunday, said Algeria's foreign currency reserves were at more than $3.5 billion this year, the highest record since 1981 because of surging oil crude prices.
World oil prices in October continued the bull run which shot crude values up 40 percent in the last four months of this year, leaving benchmark Brent at $25 a barrel, $9 above year-ago levels.
Officials said each extra $1 increase in crude prices gives Algeria a total of $500 million more hard currency gain by year.
Algeria is an OPEC member with a quota of about 750,000 barrel per day and exports of more than 30 billion cubic metres of gas each year.
Its gas imports are poised to soar shortly with the opening next week of an Algerian gas pipeline, carrying more than 8.0 billion cubic metres to Spain via Morocco and the Strait of Gibraltar.

"Monetary stabilisation, balanced finances, decline in inflation, trade liberalisation, improving trade balance and cut in the budget deficit were the factors which helped Algeria stopping growth decline and renowing with growth increase," said Keramane.

There were no figures from Keramane but earlier official figures showed Algeria's Gross Domestic Product grew by 4.4 percent in the first half of 1996 against 4.1 percent in the same period of 1995, reversing falls of 1.8 percent in 1994 and 2.9 percent in 1993.
Algeria's inflation rate fell to 19.3 percent for the year to July 1996 from 30 percent in the previous period, the government said.

Keramane foresaw an economic relaunch this year, which he said, would enable the transitional economy to face competition and spawn more jobs to absorb unemployement hitting more than two million people of the country's five million working population.

Algeria is wrestling to shift once state commanded economy to free market amid civil strife locking the government with Moslem guerrillas since early 1992 when the auhorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists were set to win.
More than 50,000 people have been killed since then and the violence spilled over to the economy with more than $2.0 billion in loss stemming from radical guerrillas sabotage.
